passage:
Jatin came home from school with his maths test folded into a tiny square. He sat on the sofa of their Delhi flat, shoulders curled, chin almost on his knees, staring at the floor.
His older sister Damini put down her book. "You look like a snail," she said.
"Leave me alone."
"Snail-Jatin. Let's play tall tree. Whoever reaches the ceiling fan first wins."
He didn't move. Then she stretched up on her toes, wobbling and making creaking tree noises. Jatin snorted. He stood up, stretched his arms high and wiggled his fingers like leaves.
After three rounds his cheeks were pink. He unfolded the test. "It's only one bad mark," he said, a bit steadier.

qa.q: How had Jatin folded his maths test?
qa.a: He had folded it into a tiny square.

qa.q: How was Jatin feeling when he came home, and what showed it?
qa.a: He was sad and a bit ashamed about the test, shown by his curled shoulders, chin near his knees and eyes on the floor.

qa.q: What did Damini try that helped?
qa.a: She turned stretching into a silly tall-tree game, which got him standing tall and moving and lifted his mood a little.

qa.q: What is it like for Damini to see her brother curled up?
qa.a: She probably feels worried for him, but she chooses play instead of pushing him to talk.

grounding: It shows a sad child hunched over after a bad test, and how playful stretching and standing tall lift his energy a little.

passage:
"Hi. Are you the new boy?"
Omkar nodded, back against the playground wall, shoulders hunched.
"I'm Nazia. We're playing statues. Want to be a statue?"
"I don't know how."
"Easy. When I shout 'freeze', you make a shape. Tall and scary, or tall and funny."
"Everyone will look at me."
"They'll be statues too. Nobody can look."
Omkar pushed himself off the wall.
"Freeze!" Nazia shouted.
Omkar stretched his arms up high like a giant, chin lifted.
"Ooh, that's a good one. What are you?"
"A... tower."
"Again, Tower! Freeze!"
This time Omkar was laughing before he stopped moving.

qa.q: What game were the children playing?
qa.a: They were playing statues.

qa.q: What was Omkar worried about when Nazia invited him?
qa.a: He was shy and worried that everyone would look at him.

qa.q: How did Nazia help Omkar join in?
qa.a: Nazia made the game sound easy, reassured him that nobody could look, and praised his tall shape.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Omkar at first?
qa.a: Nazia sees a new boy alone by the wall and wants him to feel included.

grounding: It shows a shy child hunched at the edge of the playground, and how playful movement and standing tall lift his energy.

passage:
Monday: At her new school, Shalini, nine, walked in with her shoulders hunched and her eyes on her shoes. At home she curled up small on the sofa and said, 'Nobody talks to me.'
Saturday: Urmila Maasi came to visit. 'Let's play Tall Tree!' They stretched their arms up to the ceiling, stood on tiptoe, swayed like trees in a storm and roared like lions. Shalini giggled. 'Stand like a tree and see how you feel.' Shalini stood tall. 'A bit bigger.'
The next Monday: Before assembly, Shalini remembered the tree. She lifted her chin and stood tall. She still felt shy, but when a girl in her line said hi, Shalini looked up and said hi back.

qa.q: What game did Urmila Maasi play with Shalini?
qa.a: Tall Tree.

qa.q: How was Shalini feeling on the first Monday?
qa.a: She felt lonely and small, hunching and looking at her shoes.

qa.q: What did Urmila Maasi do that helped?
qa.a: She made stretching and standing tall into a playful game, which lifted Shalini a little.

qa.q: How might the girl in the line have seen Shalini?
qa.a: She probably saw a new girl who looked up and seemed friendly enough to talk to.

grounding: Shows a shy, sad child hunching and looking down, and playful stretching and standing tall lifting her a little.

passage: Raghav, come, sit up straight for your Naveen Dada, eh? I know that slump. When I was your age, ten, in our town near Mangaluru, I was the smallest and shyest boy in class. I walked hunched over, looking at my sandals. The more I hunched, the smaller I felt. Then our PE teacher, a big laughing man named Mr D'Costa, started a game every morning. 'Everybody, be a giraffe!' We had to stretch our necks, walk on tiptoe, reach for invisible leaves. I felt silly. But one day, after being a giraffe, I noticed I was standing tall at the blackboard, and my voice came out louder. Your Dadi says I still walk like a giraffe. Now, let's see you be one.

qa.q: What was Naveen's PE teacher called?
qa.a: Mr D'Costa.

qa.q: How did young Naveen feel walking hunched over?
qa.a: Young Naveen felt shy and small, and the more he hunched, the smaller he felt.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Naveen's story?
qa.a: Playing the giraffe game every morning, which one day left Naveen standing tall and speaking louder at the blackboard.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Costa have seen the shy boys in his class?
qa.a: He probably noticed their hunched shoulders and used a silly game to help them lift up without singling anyone out.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a shy child whose hunching made him feel smaller, and how playful stretching and standing tall lifted his energy.

passage: Payal's best friend had moved to Chennai, and for a week Payal, ten, had barely lifted her head. That Sunday it poured, the power went out in the afternoon, and her aunt Jyoti found her slumped on the floor, chin on her knees. There was no TV, no phone charge, nothing to do. 'Right,' said Jyoti. 'Candle-light disco.' She sang loudly and badly. 'Arms up! Stretch! Now star jumps!' Payal rolled her eyes. Then, slowly, she stood up and stretched. Jyoti made her do a superhero pose, hands on hips, chin up. 'How does that feel?' Payal thought. 'Still sad. But a bit less small.' They danced by candlelight until the lights came back, and Payal laughed for the first time that week.

qa.q: Where had Payal's best friend moved?
qa.a: To Chennai.

qa.q: How was Payal feeling that Sunday?
qa.a: She was sad and missing her friend, slumped with her chin on her knees.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped a little?
qa.a: She turned the power cut into a playful disco with stretches, star jumps and a superhero pose.

qa.q: How might Jyoti have felt seeing Payal laugh?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and happy to see her niece laugh after a sad week.

grounding: Shows a sad child slumped and feeling small, and playful movement, stretching and standing tall lifting her energy a little.

passage: After the class photo, Ramesh walked home through Jayanagar with his shoulders curled forward and his eyes on the pavement. The photographer had called out, "Tall boy at the back, stop hunching!" and some children had giggled. At home he sat folded on the sofa like a shut umbrella. His neighbour Tenzin knocked with a skipping rope. "Come, let's see who can do fifty." Ramesh dragged himself downstairs. By the tenth jump his arms were swinging; by thirty he was laughing and standing straight to count. Tenzin's mother called from the balcony, "Look how tall you both are!" Ramesh went red, but this time he didn't shrink.

qa.q: What did Tenzin bring when knocking at the door?
qa.a: A skipping rope.

qa.q: How was Ramesh feeling on the walk home, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and small after the giggles; his shoulders curled forward and his eyes stayed on the pavement.

qa.q: Why did the skipping help Ramesh's mood?
qa.a: Playful movement got his arms swinging and his body upright, which lifted his energy and eased the shy, slumped feeling.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have noticed about Ramesh that afternoon?
qa.a: Tenzin probably saw that Ramesh looked low and folded up, and offered a game instead of questions.

grounding: Shows a shy, sad child hunching and looking down, and playful movement and standing tall lifting his energy a little.
